questions.q: State the six defining characteristics of a supermarket as per NCERT Class 11 Business Studies.
questions.a: The six characteristics are: (i) Complete line of food items and groceries plus non-food convenience goods; (ii) One-roof purchase of diverse products; (iii) Self-service principle lowering distribution cost; (iv) Lower prices due to bulk purchasing, low operational cost, and low profit margins; (v) Cash-only sales; (vi) Central location for high turnover. A wrong answer that omits "cash-only" or "self-service" reveals the student confuses supermarkets with departmental stores, which offer credit and personal service.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why supermarkets operate on a cash-only basis and how this feature creates both an advantage and a limitation for the business.
questions.a: Cash-only eliminates bad debts and reduces working capital blocked in receivables, lowering operational cost and enabling lower prices (advantage). However, it excludes customers who rely on credit for large purchases, restricting purchasing power and limiting the customer base to those with immediate liquidity (limitation). A wrong answer that only states "no bad debts" without linking to lower prices or excluding credit-dependent customers shows superficial understanding of the trade-off.

questions.q: A supermarket in a Tier-2 Indian city stocks 15,000 SKUs. The average markup on food items is 8% and on non-food items is 15%. If food items constitute 65% of sales revenue and non-food 35%, calculate the overall gross profit margin percentage. If the supermarket's monthly fixed overheads (rent, salaries, utilities) are ₹12 lakh, what minimum monthly sales revenue is required to break even? Assume no other variable costs.
questions.a:
Step 1: Weighted average gross margin = (0.65 × 8%) + (0.35 × 15%) = 5.2% + 5.25% = 10.45%.
Step 2: Break-even sales = Fixed overheads ÷ Gross margin = ₹12,00,000 ÷ 0.1045 = ₹1,14,83,253 (approx ₹1.15 crore).
A wrong answer using simple average (11.5%) or ignoring the revenue-mix weighting reveals the student cannot apply weighted averages to retail profitability analysis—a key board exam skill.

questions.q: Compare and contrast supermarkets and discount stores on the following dimensions: (a) Product assortment breadth vs. depth; (b) Location strategy; (c) Service level; (d) Pricing philosophy. Use Indian examples (e.g., DMart vs. Reliance Smart vs. a hypothetical discount store).
questions.a: Supermarkets (DMart, Reliance Smart): Broad assortment (food + non-food), moderate depth per category; central/high-traffic locations; self-service with minimal assistance; everyday low pricing (EDLP) on groceries. Discount stores (hypothetical Indian equivalent of Walmart's early model or Value Bazaar): Narrower assortment focused on high-turnover branded goods, deeper stock in selected categories; peripheral/low-rent locations; bare-bones service (no bags, no trolleys sometimes); aggressive discounting below MRP via volume leverage. A wrong answer that treats them as identical or swaps location strategies shows failure to analyse how cost structure drives format design.

questions.q: "Supermarkets are unsuitable for selling high-value, high-involvement products like laptops, jewellery, or customised furniture." Evaluate this statement with three arguments for and two counter-arguments, referencing specific supermarket features.
questions.a: Arguments for: (1) Self-service denies expert consultation needed for complex products; (2) Cash-only limits high-ticket purchases; (3) Open-shelf display risks theft/damage for valuables. Counter-arguments: (1) Some Indian supermarkets (e.g., Big Bazaar) have dedicated electronics sections with demo units and EMI tie-ups, mitigating (1) and (2); (2) Locked glass cabinets and security tags can secure high-value items while retaining footfall. A one-sided answer missing counter-arguments or ignoring Indian adaptations shows inability to evaluate context-dependent retail strategy.

questions.q: Give the correct order of design decisions in a hybrid format that blends supermarket efficiency with kirana convenience.
questions.a: The design runs: (1) Stock high-frequency low-involvement goods such as staples, fresh produce and daily-use items (2) Run assisted self-service with staff who guide elderly customers (3) Take cash and UPI plus weekly credit for verified local residents (4) Locate near residential clusters and add short-range home delivery for local orders. A wrong answer that copies the cash-only rule untouched shows the student has missed that a hybrid must soften each supermarket limitation that the kirana customarily solves.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: A supermarket is a large-scale retail ______ operating on a self-service basis, offering a wide assortment of food, grocery, and non-food consumer goods at relatively low prices through bulk purchasing, low operational costs, and low profit margins, with sales conducted strictly on a cash-and-carry basis.

Fill in the blank: Imagine you walk into a Big Bazaar or DMart on a weekend: you pick up a trolley, navigate aisles labelled "Staples," "Fresh Produce," "Home Care," select branded items with visible price tags, and pay at a checkout counter—no ______ persuades you, no credit is offered, and you carry bags home.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student must be able to: (1) Distinguish supermarkets and discount stores from departmental stores and chain stores using at least four differentiating features with Indian examples; (2) Evaluate the suitability of each format for specific product categories and consumer segments by analysing the trade-offs between price, service.
